title: Transformer Models for Clinical Text Classification
abstract: Background: Clinical notes contain valuable information but are difficult to analyze at scale. Objective: We evaluate transformer models for classifying clinical text. Methods: We compare BERT and baseline machine learning models using a held-out dataset and macro F1. Results: The transformer model improves macro F1 over baselines. Conclusion: Contextual representations may support clinical text classification.

title: A Review of Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare
abstract: Background: Explainability is important when AI supports clinical decisions. Objective: This review maps explainable AI methods used in healthcare. Methods: We searched four bibliographic databases and screened studies using predefined criteria. Results: Feature attribution and example-based explanations were common, while prospective evaluations were rare. Conclusion: More clinically grounded evaluation is needed.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Citation Recommendation
abstract: We study graph neural networks for recommending scholarly references. We construct a citation graph, compare graph-based methods with content-based baselines, and evaluate ranking quality using NDCG and Recall. The proposed approach improves ranking on two benchmark collections. These findings suggest that graph structure can complement textual similarity.

title: Open Science Practices and Research Visibility
abstract: Background: Open science is increasingly discussed as a way to improve research transparency. Objective: We examine associations between open access, data sharing, and citation counts. Methods: We analyze a cross-sectional sample of publications and fit multivariable regression models. Results: Open access and data availability are positively associated with citations, though estimates vary by field and publication age. Conclusion: Observational associations should not be interpreted as causal effects.

title: Sentiment Analysis of Short Social Media Messages
abstract: This paper explores sentiment analysis for short social media posts. Several classifiers are tested and results are compared. The best model performs well. We discuss limitations and possible future work.

title: Systematic Mapping of Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Background: Retrieval-augmented generation combines external evidence with language generation. Objective: We systematically map evaluation practices for retrieval-augmented generation systems. Methods: We searched scholarly indexes, applied inclusion criteria, and coded datasets, retrieval metrics, and faithfulness measures. Results: Evaluation protocols differ substantially and evidence-grounding measures are inconsistently reported. Conclusion: Shared benchmarks and transparent reporting could improve comparability.

title: Predicting Protein Function from Sequence Embeddings
abstract: Background: Protein function prediction remains challenging for understudied proteins. Objective: We assess sequence embeddings for function prediction. Methods: We compare embedding-based classifiers with profile-based baselines across three datasets. Results: Embeddings improve macro F1 on two datasets but not on the most distant test set. Conclusion: Generalization remains a key challenge.

title: Machine Learning for Urban Air Quality Forecasting
abstract: Urban air pollution creates serious public health concerns. This study uses machine learning to forecast air quality from sensor data. We test several algorithms and report their accuracy. Results indicate that the proposed model is useful for prediction.

title: Bias Auditing in Automated Hiring Systems
abstract: Background: Automated hiring tools can reproduce or amplify unequal outcomes. Objective: We evaluate demographic performance differences in resume-screening models. Methods: We define group-wise error metrics and audit three model families on a controlled benchmark. Results: Error disparities persist across models and depend on job category and threshold choice. Conclusion: Audits should report subgroup uncertainty and document deployment context.

title: Topic Models for Historical Newspaper Archives
abstract: We investigate topic models for exploring digitized newspaper archives. We compare latent Dirichlet allocation with neural topic models using coherence scores and a small expert review. Neural methods yield higher semantic coherence but are less stable across random seeds. We release a reproducible evaluation protocol.

title: Forecasting Hospital Readmissions with Tabular Data
abstract: Background: Hospital readmissions create costs for health systems. Objective: We develop a readmission risk model. Methods: We train logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting models on retrospective records. Results: Gradient boosting achieves the highest AUROC. Conclusion: External validation is required before clinical use.

title: Low-Resource Machine Translation with Data Augmentation
abstract: Background: Low-resource languages often lack parallel training data. Objective: We evaluate data augmentation for neural machine translation. Methods: We compare back-translation and multilingual transfer on three language pairs using BLEU and chrF. Results: Augmentation improves translation quality for two pairs but has mixed effects for the third. Conclusion: Strategy selection should account for language-specific data conditions.
